profile.name: PostHog
profile.summary: PostHog is a product context layer that ingests and stores analytics, errors, replays, and business data so teams and AI agents can query and act on it.
problems: Product and company data is scattered across analytics, errors, replays, business data, support tickets, and external tools.
AI agents lack product context and teams have to context-switch to a browser to query product data.
Teams need to investigate conversion drops and funnel issues across ads, payments, and code changes.
Session replays reveal dead clicks, quick backs, long stalls, checkout issues, and payment retries.
Error tracking is needed to group exceptions and stack traces, including mobile sign-in failures.
Teams need feature flags, experiments, no-code A/B testing, surveys, and feedback tools.
A data warehouse and CDP are needed to pipe in third-party data from many sources for a complete picture.
Self-driving inbox findings need to be clustered into prioritized reports and pull requests.
Teams need logs, tracing, AI observability, heatmaps, replay vision, and other built-in tools for agents.
Setup and querying should work from the terminal, editor, desktop, Slack, or web app without new UI.
profile.ideal_customer: Product, engineering, data, and AI-agent teams at software companies that need one place to ingest, query, and act on product and company data, from free-tier startups to teams scaling usage.

leads.title: Analytics has changed. Here's what to do about it
leads.content:
- Use the wrong definition for a term like “sign ups” or “MRR.” We asked Claude, Cursor, and PostHog AI “what’s our MRR last month?” and got three different queries and answers.
- Do their own math and mess up the calculation. An MCP-heavy user told us experiment numbers didn’t match the UI because the agent was writing its own query.
- Use the wrong column or property. A question about AI crawler errors returned an 0% error rate because it used status\_code rather than proxy\_status\_code (which shows a 1% error rate).

You, your agents, your colleagues, and their agents will assume they are right and there’s no gatekeepers (like a data team) to say they’re wrong. [...] - Tagging key events with an agent or human source. At PostHog, backend events like dashboard created or experiment created get a source property with values like web, mcp, slack, and cli. This is how we know 50% of dashboards and 18% of experiments are created using AI.
- MCP Analytics. Our SDK captures every tool call as an $mcp\_tool\_call. It provides clients, error rates, latency, and intent. Through this we’ve found many missing capabilities as well as broken ones, like agents telling us they couldn’t resolve or archive error tracking issues. [...] - What are the events we actually care about? We have collected 14 events and 72 sign up related actions, but only two are “approved” through our semantic layer.
- Are they accurate? Replay activation is an event we care about, and we saw it falling over the last four months, when we realized it didn’t account for MCP users, so it needed rewriting.
- What does good look like? A scorecard says gross revenue retention above 80% is healthy for mature products and monthly logo churn below 2.5% is green.
- Codifying definitions and gotchas.Skills and our semantic layer is how we do this. For example, our revenue analysis skill mentions that “upcoming” invoices are full-period projections, not settled revenue and credited startups read $0 until credits run out.

leads.title: Fix Session Replay Sampling Bias
leads.content:
The correct priority may be the issue with the smallest replay count.

A useful replay program therefore asks two separate questions:

1. How frequently does the issue occur in the relevant population?
2. How much customer or revenue value is exposed when it occurs?

A practical prioritization score can be expressed as:

Estimated affected sessions × conversion opportunity × expected value × confidence

This is not accounting-grade attribution. It is a better decision model than sorting recordings by issue count.

### Do not “fix” bias by recording everything

Increasing the recording rate can reduce random sampling error, but it does not automatically remove systematic bias. [...] Use a repeatable workflow:

01. Select one decision and one customer population.
02. Review the segment's replay coverage against analytics.
03. Watch a random set before applying issue filters.
04. Watch targeted sets for errors, abandonment, latency, and experiment exposure.
05. Code observations using a consistent friction taxonomy.
06. Estimate affected sessions using known sampling probabilities.
07. Add conversion opportunity and value exposure.
08. Validate the proposed cause with quantitative data.
09. Release the fix with an experiment or measurable before-and-after design.
10. Check whether the expected customer and revenue outcome changed.

This turns session replay from a video library into a decision system.

### The metric that matters is not recordings watched [...] ### Analyst attention bias

People prefer dramatic recordings. A chaotic session feels more informative than a quiet abandonment.

But the session with no clicks after the pricing page may be the commercially important one.

### The revenue problem hidden inside raw replay counts

Suppose a team finds these issues in its watched sessions:

- 28 sessions contain repeated navigation clicks
- 11 sessions contain a form validation error
- 4 sessions contain a payment failure

The raw count makes navigation look like the priority.

Now add business context:

- The navigation issue affects content readers with no purchase intent
- The validation issue affects demo requests worth an estimated $800 each
- The payment issue affects carts averaging $1,200

leads.title: Session Replay After A/B Tests: Find Lost Revenue
leads.content:
### Quantify the Behavioral Pattern Before Prioritizing It

After replay reveals a pattern, define a trackable behavioral signature.

For example:

- First validation error occurs after payment interaction
- User returns from payment to order summary
- More than one click occurs on the collapsed summary label
- Purchase does not occur within the exposed session

Then compare the rate of that signature between variants.

Assume:

- 10,000 users were exposed to each variant
- 8% of Variant B sessions showed checkout backtracking
- 3% of control sessions showed the same behavior
- The conversion rate was 22% without the behavior and 9% with it
- Average order value was $120

Variant B produced 500 excess backtracking sessions:

`10,000 × (8% − 3%) = 500 excess sessions` [...] Look for duplicate success events, thank-you page reloads, missing transaction confirmation, unexpected redirects, and variant tags that disagree with the visual treatment.

### Use a Replay Coding Framework

For each reviewed session, record a small, consistent set of observations:

- Experiment key and variant
- Exposure confirmed: yes or no
- Primary task attempted: yes or no
- Outcome completed: yes or no
- Friction category
- Step where friction first appeared
- Severity: low, medium, or high
- Evidence timestamp or replay moment
- Tracking mismatch: yes or no
- Recommended action: ignore, investigate, fix, or retest

Two reviewers should independently code a subset of sessions. If they routinely disagree, the categories are too vague or the evidence is too weak. [...] Did the experience break rather than persuade poorly?

Look for missing components, flicker, layout shift, unresponsive controls, validation loops, loading states that never resolve, and browser-specific defects.

### 5. Trust failure

Did the new design remove cues that made the original experience feel safe or familiar?

Look for hesitation before payment, repeated review of totals, attempts to find security or return information, and exits immediately after a surprising fee appears.

### 6. Measurement failure

Did the user complete the desired action while analytics failed to record it, or did analytics record an outcome that the replay does not support?

leads.title: How Agoda is evolving engineering support with AI agents
leads.content:
The same BI Product team mentioned earlier also uses a pipeline that reviews recent negative feedback and proposes skill updates through an MR. A human reviews each change before it is merged.

### Invest in error analysis

Understanding an agent requires time and good observability. Traces show the path it followed, the tools it called, and where the investigation failed. Without them, explaining a “not useful” response would be difficult.

Error analysis also exposed limitations around the agent. When Slack was unavailable, we introduced FeedMCP to monitor its status feed and those of similar SaaS services.

When a Tempo query returned a 12 MB response and exceeded the agent’s context window, we began experimenting with tool-side summarisation, code mode, and sub-agents. [...] Agent Eval replays the saved cases through the Agents Platform and records the answers and tool calls. For each case, teams define the behaviour they want to check. They might assess the answer, require a particular tool call, or verify selected tool arguments. Running the same dataset against the current and proposed versions makes it easier to see how a change affects the agent.

We are also working towards shadow evaluation. This sends the same live request to two agent versions in parallel. The current version answers the requester, while the candidate version is evaluated without its response being shown. Teams can then assess the candidate using real traffic before releasing it.

## Where we go next

leads.title: Guidely — Product analytics, in-app guides and feedback in one SDK | Gurp Parmar | 12 comments
leads.content:
Most products need five tools to help users: one for onboarding, one for support chat, one for session replay, one for error tracking and one for feature flags. ⠀ That's five SDKs in your app, five contracts, five bills, and five vendors who each know a different slice of the same user. ⠀ We built Guidely so it's one: ⠀ → Product tours, checklists and surveys you build by clicking your own app → Scout, an AI messenger that answers from your help articles → Complaints routed to the right team → Step-by-step how-tos (and videos) recorded in one take → Feature flags and A/B tests → Native guides on iOS and Android → Session replay, heatmaps, funnels and error tracking ⠀ One SDK and one bill. It's free to start with no card, then pay as you go: guides are never metered, there's no per-seat [...] The biggest benefit of consolidating these tools may be less about having one bill and more about reducing the integration work between them. The key is whether teams can get that simplicity without losing the depth of analytics and control they rely on.

Five SDKs for one user is the real cost — size, contracts, and five different pictures of the same session. One SDK is the pitch. Native iOS/Android guides is the part most of these tools still fake with a webview.

five vendors each owning a slice of the user journey is the hidden tax here. one sdk that covers tours, support and replay is the kind of consolidation teams actually feel week to week.

leads.content:
### What Tool for What Job?

| Need | Tool Category | Recommendations |
 --- 
| "What are users doing?" | Product Analytics | Amplitude, Mixpanel, PostHog |
| "Why is this page slow?" | Performance Monitoring | Web Vitals + Sentry Perf / Datadog RUM |
| "What happened before the crash?" | Error Tracking + Replay | Sentry (errors) + LogRocket/FullStory (replay) |
| "Where are users clicking?" | Heatmaps | Hotjar, Microsoft Clarity (free) |
| "Is the new design better?" | A/B Testing | LaunchDarkly, Statsig, PostHog |
| "Can I ship this safely?" | Feature Flags | LaunchDarkly, Unleash, Flagsmith |
| "What's in the logs?" | Log Management | ELK, Loki+Grafana, Datadog Logs |
| "User reported a bug" | Session Replay | FullStory, LogRocket, Sentry Replay |

### Startup vs Enterprise Stack [...] ### 4.4 Tools Compared

| Tool | Session Replay | Heatmaps | Analytics | Error Tracking | Pricing |
 ---  ---  --- |
| Hotjar | ✅ | ✅ Click, Scroll, Move | Basic | ❌ | Free tier / $$ |
| FullStory | ✅ (best) | ✅ | ✅ | ✅ | $$$$ |
| LogRocket | ✅ | ❌ | ✅ | ✅ (Redux, network) | $$$ |
| PostHog | ✅ | ✅ | ✅ | ❌ | Free (self-host) / $$ |
| Microsoft Clarity | ✅ | ✅ Click, Scroll | Basic | ❌ | Free |

| Heap | ✅ | ❌ | ✅ (auto-capture) | ❌ | $$$ |

💡 Microsoft Clarity is a great free option for session replay + heatmaps. It uses rrweb under the hood and integrates with Google Analytics.

## Frontend Error Tracking and Debugging

### 5.1 Types of Frontend Errors [...] ⬆ Back to Top

## Putting It All Together Unified Observability

In production, these systems are interconnected:

`User Action
│
├──→ Analytics: track('product_added_to_cart', { ... })
│
├──→ Feature Flag: useFeatureFlag('new_cart_animation')
│
├──→ A/B Test: experiment exposure tracked
│
├──→ Logger: logger.info('cart_updated', { itemCount: 3 })
│
└──→ Error (if any): Sentry captures with breadcrumbs + replay
All connected by:
• sessionId — groups all events from one visit
• userId — groups all events from one user
• traceId — connects frontend request to backend span
• release — associates events with a specific deploy`

# Replayable Agent Runs: The Debugging Trick That Ships

## How deterministic replays turn “it worked yesterday” agents into reliable products you can fix, audit, and trust.

Learn how replaying agent runs enables deterministic debugging, safer tool calls, and shippable reliability with traces, snapshots, and step-by-step re-execution.

Let’s be real: the first time you watch an agent fail in production, you stop thinking about prompts and start thinking about forensics.

Because the failure isn’t polite. It’s not a clean stack trace. It’s a messy mix of: a slightly different tool response, a flaky network call, a model choosing a different path, and your team staring at logs that read like modern poetry.

And then someone asks the question that changes everything:

> “Can we replay it?” [...] So your logs show:

- partial prompts
- scattered tool responses
- missing context
- no stable “state” you can step through

That’s why “just add more logging” rarely helps. What you need is the ability to reconstruct the run.

Replaying is how you go from storytelling to evidence.

## What “replaying an agent run” actually means

A replay is the ability to re-execute an agent session step-by-step using the same inputs, the same tool responses (or controlled substitutions), and the same intermediate state — so you can reproduce what happened.

Think of it like:

- flight recorder (you capture what happened)
- plus time machine (you can rerun it)
- plus debugger (you can pause, inspect, change one variable, and continue)

## Two types of replays you should support [...] In other words: replay is the bridge between “cool demo” and “real product.”

## Conclusion: if you can’t replay it, you can’t ship it

Agents are interactive systems with moving parts. Moving parts require reproducibility.

Start small:

- route all tools through a gateway
- record tool requests and responses
- add step IDs and run IDs
- support deterministic replay in your dev environment

Then build up to snapshots and diff-based experiments.

If you’re building agents right now, comment with your stack (LangGraph, custom Node runtime, OpenAI function calls, etc.) and what tools you’re calling. I’ll suggest a minimal replay architecture that fits your setup. Follow for more practical, production-grade agent patterns.

leads.title: Deep dive into context engineering for AI agents
leads.content:
For discrete tasks with clear inputs and outputs, agents should usually communicate through artefacts rather than raw traces. A web-search agent, for instance, does not need to pass along its entire browsing history. It only needs to surface the material that downstream agents can actually use.

This means that intermediate reasoning, failed attempts, and exploration traces stay private unless explicitly needed. What gets passed forward are distilled outputs: extracted facts, validated findings, or decisions that constrain the next step.

For more tightly coupled tasks, like a debugging agent where downstream reasoning genuinely depends on prior attempts, a limited form of trace sharing can be introduced. But this should be deliberate and scoped, not the default.

### KV cache penalty [...] Image 5

Drawn by author

Once you look at real agent systems this way, a lot of supposed “model failures” now look different. I’ve encountered many of such at work. These are actually harness failures: the agent forgot because nothing persisted the right state; it repeated work because the harness surfaced no durable artefact of prior failure; it chose the wrong tool because the harness overloaded the action space; and so on.

A good harness is, in some sense, a deterministic shell wrapped around a stochastic core. It makes the context legible, stable, and recoverable enough that the model can spend its limited reasoning budget on the task rather than on reconstructing its own state from a messy trace.

## Communication between agents [...] In practice, good context engineering usually comes down to four moves. You offload information to external systems (context offloading) so the model does not need to carry everything in-band. You retrieve information dynamically instead of front-loading all of it (context retrieval). You isolate context so one subtask does not contaminate another (context isolation). And you reduce history when needed, but only in ways that preserve what the agent will still need later (context reduction).

A common failure mode on the other side is context pollution: the presence of too much unnecessary, conflicting or redundant information that it distracts the LLM.

### Context rot

So you can see web scraping isn’t a “set it and forget it” task. It requires maintenance. You need to be prepared for the fact that websites change, and your code will need to adapt to keep the data flowing.

## Method 1. The No-Code Route

Not everyone is a Python wizard, and honestly, you don’t always need to be one to get data.

If writing code sounds intimidating, visual scraping platforms are a fantastic entry point. I often tell beginners to look into tools like Octoparse or ParseHub. The concept is simple: if you can browse the web, you can scrape it. It’s mostly a “point-and-click” experience where you highlight the data you want on the screen, and the software figures out the rest. [...] For even simpler tasks, like grabbing a table from a single webpage, browser extensions like Instant Data Scraper can work wonders. You just fire it up, and it detects the data structure instantly.

But here’s my honest take on the pros and cons:

- The Good Stuff: The learning curve is practically non-existent. You can go from “I need data” to “I have a CSV file” in minutes without writing a single line of code. It’s a huge time-saver for testing ideas.
- The Catch: While they are easy to use, they can feel a bit like bowling with bumpers. You lose flexibility. If you need to do something highly specific or complex, you might find yourself hitting the software’s limits. Also, keep an eye on your budget — while many offer free tiers, the costs can stack up quickly if you try to scale up. [...] ### Step 1. Import the Libraries

First things first, we need to bring in our tools. We’ll need `requests` to actually visit the webpage and `BeautifulSoup` to parse the HTML so we can find the data we want. I also import `csv` so we can save our hard work later.

`import requests from bs4 import BeautifulSoup import csv`

### Step 2. Fetch and Parse the Page

Now, let’s send a request to the target website. This is the digital equivalent of typing a URL into your browser and hitting Enter.

Once we get the response, we check if the status code is `200` (which means "Success!" in web-speak). If it is, we pass the raw HTML content to BeautifulSoup to make sense of it.
